projects.name: Hybrid VQC Weather Forecasting with FPGA Inference
projects.blurb: 7-qubit variational circuit for temperature forecasting, with a custom kernel on an AMD Alveo FPGA for low-latency inference.
projects.abstract: A hybrid quantum-classical pipeline that forecasts temperature using a 7-qubit variational quantum circuit (50 parameters). The trained inference kernel is compiled to an AMD Alveo U55C FPGA using HLS with HBM memory, reaching 291.8 µs inference — a 6.7× speedup over GPU execution — and is wired into CI/CD for continuous testing.
projects.role: Lead developer — algorithm design, training pipeline, and FPGA deployment.

sections.p: Classical statistical baselines for short-horizon temperature forecasting plateau quickly on limited sensor data. The open question was whether a variational quantum circuit could extract more signal — and, if so, whether it could run fast enough to matter operationally.

I designed a 7-qubit variational quantum circuit with 50 trainable parameters, using angle encoding to map meteorological features into the circuit and a hardware-efficient ansatz to keep depth tractable. The classical optimiser and the quantum layer were wired into a single hybrid training loop, implemented in Qiskit and PennyLane.

Inference latency, not training, is the operational bottleneck. I compiled the trained kernel to an AMD Alveo U55C FPGA using HLS, placing circuit parameters in HBM to keep memory access off the critical path. The result was 291.8 µs per inference — 6.7× faster than GPU execution of the same kernel.

The whole pipeline runs under CI/CD: circuit changes trigger retraining, regression tests on forecast accuracy, and a rebuild of the FPGA bitstream. This is what makes the result reproducible rather than a one-off benchmark.
56.5% improvement over statistical baselines, with inference fast enough for operational deployment. Accepted at IEEE TQCEBT 2026.

projects.name: Quantum Image Representation Neural Networks
projects.blurb: Quantum neural networks for binary image classification built on four quantum image encodings: NASS, QBIR, FTQR and FRQCI.
projects.abstract: Quantum neural networks that classify binary MNIST images (0 vs 1) at 2×2, 4×4 and 8×8, with pixel data encoded through four quantum image representations: NASS, QBIR, FTQR and FRQCI. Published in The Journal of Supercomputing 82 (2026).

sections.p: Quantum image classification depends heavily on how classical pixel data is encoded into quantum states, but encodings are often chosen by convention rather than by measured trade-off.
I built quantum neural networks on four quantum image representations — NASS, QBIR, FTQR and FRQCI — for binary MNIST classification (0 vs 1) at 2×2, 4×4 and 8×8.
Published in The Journal of Supercomputing 82 (2026).

projects.name: Linear-Optical QKD Network Testbeds
projects.blurb: DPS, COW, and Twin-Field QKD simulated over realistic photonic channels with security analysis.
projects.abstract: Simulation testbeds for differential-phase-shift (DPS), coherent-one-way (COW), and Twin-Field QKD protocols over lossy, noisy photonic channels. Includes security analysis against intercept-resend and photon-number-splitting attacks, plus Python tooling for optical simulation post-processing.
projects.role: Research fellow — simulation design, security analysis, and tooling.

sections.p: QKD protocols are usually analysed under idealised channel assumptions. Deployment behaviour depends on loss, detector noise, and attacker models that idealised analysis omits.

I built simulation testbeds for three protocols — differential-phase-shift (DPS), coherent-one-way (COW), and Twin-Field QKD — in OptiSystem and ANSYS, modelling realistic photonic loss and noise across the channel.

Each protocol was evaluated against intercept-resend and photon-number-splitting attacks, with key-rate degradation quantified as a function of channel loss. I also benchmarked resource-state and entanglement generation.
Optical simulators produce large, awkward output. I wrote Python post-processing tooling to make the analysis reusable and maintainable rather than a manual per-run effort.

projects.name: Quantum Circuits for Block Ciphers
projects.blurb: Mini-AES / S-AES circuits with a Grover-based chosen-ciphertext attack demonstration.
projects.abstract: Quantum circuit designs for Mini-AES and S-AES block ciphers with Galois-field arithmetic, validated on Qiskit simulators and IBM Quantum hardware. Demonstrates a chosen-ciphertext attack via Grover's search and amplitude amplification.
projects.role: Research intern — circuit design and attack demonstration.

sections.p: Understanding how symmetric ciphers degrade under quantum attack requires explicit, runnable circuit constructions, not just asymptotic arguments.
I designed quantum circuits for Mini-AES and S-AES, including the Galois-field arithmetic that the S-box depends on, and validated them on Qiskit simulators and IBM Quantum hardware.
I demonstrated a chosen-ciphertext attack using Grover's search with amplitude amplification, making the quadratic speedup concrete on a scaled-down cipher.
Work also covered circuit optimisation and error-correction considerations for running these constructions on noisy devices.

projects.name: Entanglement Detection via Neural Networks (NMR)
projects.blurb: ANN models for multipartite entanglement detection and SLOCC classification in NMR qubits.
projects.abstract: Neural-network models that detect genuine multipartite entanglement and classify SLOCC classes in 2- and 3-qubit NMR systems, trained on reconstructed density matrices. Published in Quantum Information Processing (Springer).
projects.role: MS research student — model design and experimental analysis.

sections.p: Detecting genuine multipartite entanglement in experimental NMR systems is hard: witnesses are state-specific and reconstructed density matrices are noisy.
I trained neural-network models to detect genuine multipartite entanglement and classify SLOCC classes in 2- and 3-qubit NMR systems, using experimentally reconstructed density matrices as input.
Alongside the models I performed density-matrix reconstruction and quantum error modelling, applying PCA, MCA, and LDA to characterise the structure of the quantum datasets.
Published in Quantum Information Processing (Springer).

about.headline: Bridging quantum theory and shipped software.
statement: My work sits at the seam between quantum information research and production engineering. I am interested in the question of what it actually takes to move a quantum algorithm off a whiteboard and onto hardware that runs under real constraints — noise, latency, memory bandwidth, and the unglamorous requirement that it keep working next week.

That has led me across three connected areas. In variational quantum algorithms and quantum machine learning, I study how circuit structure and data encoding govern trainability and expressivity, and how hybrid pipelines can beat classical baselines on real forecasting tasks. In quantum hardware acceleration, I compile trained quantum kernels down to FPGA fabric, where a 6.7× speedup over GPUs is a systems-engineering result as much as a quantum one. In photonic quantum networks, I simulate QKD protocols over lossy channels and analyse their security against realistic attacks.

What connects them is a conviction that quantum computing progresses fastest when research artefacts are built like software — tested, versioned, reproducible, and deployable. I want to keep working where those two cultures meet.
